The body of the Emperor was secretly entrusted to Takechi no Sukune, who removed it by sea to Anato and buried it temporarily in the Palace of Toyora with a fireless temporary burial, for the sake of secrecy no lights being used; that year, owing to the expedition against Silla, it was impossible to bury the Emperor properly.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book VIII, secs. 8-9 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

title.en: The Seven-Night Divination: Jingu Names the Gods Who Spoke
title.zh: 神功皇后彈琴迎神，七日七夜知神名

region.en: Palace of worship at Wayamada, Tsukushi

source.work: Nihongi (Chronicles of Japan), Vol. I, trans. W. G. Aston (1896)

summary.en: Grieved that Chūai died refusing the divine instructions, the Empress commissions purification and a Palace of worship at Wayamada, herself discharging the priest's office while Takechi no Sukune plays the lute. For seven days and nights the gods answer one by one: the deity of Ise representing herself as a Corean deity, the eulalia deity, the awful Koto-shiro-nushi, and the three water-gods of Hiuga. The Kumaso submit at once when Kamo no Wake is sent against them.
summary.zh: 神功皇后以帝不從神誨而早崩，欲知降禍之神，乃修祓築齋宮於山田，親為齋主，武內宿禰撫琴，中臣烏子為齋部。以千縈之幣置琴上祈曰前日誨帝者何神。七日七夜乃有答：伊勢五十鈴宮之神自稱，又有出於芻茅之耳之神，又有統理天地虛空之事代主神，又有日向橘小戶水底之三神。既得神名依誨奉祭，遣賀茂別命擊熊襲，不日而降。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Nihongi); passages are condensed paraphrases of the public-domain Aston translation, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: At this time the Empress was grieved that the Emperor would not follow the Divine instructions, and had consequently died a premature death. She thought she would find out what God had sent the curse, so that she might possess herself of the land of treasures. She therefore commanded her ministers and functionaries to purge offences and rectify transgressions, and to construct a Palace of worship in the village of Wayamada. The Empress, having selected a lucky day, entered the Palace of worship and discharged in person the office of priest. She commanded Takechi no Sukune to play on the lute, and the Nakatomi Ikatsu no Omi was designated as Saniha, the official who examines the utterances prompted by the Deity. Then placing one thousand pieces of cloth, high pieces of cloth, on the top and bottom of the lute, she prayed, saying: 'Who is the God who on a former day instructed the Emperor? I pray that I may know his name.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book IX, secs. 1-3 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: After seven days and seven nights there came an answer, saying: 'I am the Deity who dwells in the Shrine of split-bell Isuzu in the district of hundred-transmit Watarahi in the province of divine-wind Ise, and my name is Tsuki-sakaki idzu no mi-tama ama-zakaru Muka-tsu hime no Mikoto' - the Sun-Goddess choosing to represent herself as a Corean Deity. Again she inquired whether other Deities were present.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book IX, secs. 3-4 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: The answer was: 'I am the Deity who comes forth on the ears of the flag-like Eulalia, and my dwelling is in the district of Aha in Ada-fushi in Oda.' She inquired: 'Are there others?' There was an answer, saying: 'There is the Deity who rules in Heaven, who rules in the Void, the gem-casket-entering-prince, the awful Koto-shiro-nushi.' Asked whether there were others, the Saniha said there was no answer now but they would speak again afterwards; then came the answer: 'There are the Gods who have settled to the bottom of the water of the Little Strait of Tachibana in the Land of Hiuga, who are produced and dwell there like fresh water plants. Their names are Uha-tsutsu no wo, Naka-tsutsu no wo, and Soko-tsutsu no wo.' Nothing more was ever said as to the existence of other Gods.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book IX, secs. 3-4 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: Now that the Divine words had been obtained, the Gods were worshipped in accordance with their instructions. Thereafter Kamo no Wake, the ancestor of the Kibi no Omi, was sent to attack the Kumaso, and before many days had elapsed they freely submitted.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book IX, sec. 4 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

title.en: The Needle-Hook of Matsura and the Thunder-Split Rock
title.zh: 針作釣鉤得鱒，雷劈石通神田溝

source.work: Nihongi (Chronicles of Japan), Vol. I, trans. W. G. Aston (1896)

summary.en: On the bank of the river Wogawa the Empress bends a needle into a hook, baits it with grains of rice, makes a line from the threads of her garment, and standing on a stone mid-stream prays: if the westward quest for the Land of Treasure is to succeed, let the fish bite. She raises the rod and catches a trout, and Matsura is named from medzura, strange. Ever after the women of the land cast hooks each fourth month; men may angle but catch nothing. A great rock blocks the channel of a sacred rice-field; prayer with sword and mirror brings thunder that splits the rock.
summary.zh: 皇后至肥前玉嶋小河畔，曲針作鉤，取米粒為餌，抽衣縷為線，立於河中石上投鉤祈曰「西行求寶國，若成，令魚上鉤」。舉竿得鱒。時人異之，名其國曰松浦。故每歲四月上旬，其國婦人皆持鉤釣鱒，至今不絕；男子雖釣而無所得。又為御田開渠，大石塞之，乃召武內宿禰持劍鏡禱天地，忽有雷雨劈石而水通，因名曰裂田溝。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Nihongi); passages are condensed paraphrases of the public-domain Aston translation, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Proceeding northwards, she arrived at the district of Matsura in the Land of Hizen, and partook of food on the bank of the river Wogawa in the village of Tamashima. Here the Empress bent a needle and made of it a hook. She took grains of rice and used them as bait. Pulling out the threads of her garment, she made of them a line. Then mounting upon a stone in the middle of the river and casting the hook, she prayed, saying: 'We are proceeding westward, where we desire to gain possession of the Land of Treasure.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book IX, sec. 6 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: If we are to succeed, let the fish of the river bite the hook.' Accordingly, raising up her fishing-rod, she caught a trout. Then the Empress said: 'It is a strange thing.' Wherefore the men of the day called that place the Land of Medzura - the present name Matsura is a corruption of this. For this reason, whenever the first decade of the fourth month comes round, the women of that land take hooks, which they cast into the river and catch trout - a custom which has not ceased unto this day. The men may angle for fish, but they cannot catch any.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book IX, sec. 6 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: This having been done, the Empress knew that there was virtue in the teaching of the Gods, and she made sacrifice anew to the Gods of Heaven and Earth. As it was her purpose in person to chastise the West, she set apart a sacred rice-field and tilled it. Then, in order to divert water from the Naka-gaha with which to irrigate it, she dug a channel as far as the Hill of Todoroki. But a great rock stood in the way, and she was unable to pierce a channel through it. Then the Empress sent for Takechi no Sukune, and offering a sword and a mirror made him pray to the Gods of Heaven and Earth to allow the channel to be completed. Straightway there came thunder and lightning, and split that rock asunder, so that the water passed through. Therefore the men of the time called that channel the Channel of Sakuta.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book IX, sec. 6 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

title.en: Jingu's Conquest of Silla: The Tide That Followed the Ships
title.zh: 神功西征新羅：潮水隨船而入

region.en: Sea crossing from Tsukushi to Silla (Tsushima Strait, symbolic pin)
region.zh: 自筑紫渡海征新羅（對馬海峽，象徵錨點）

source.work: Nihongi (Chronicles of Japan), Vol. I, trans. W. G. Aston (1896)

summary.en: The Empress bathes in the sea and vows that if her hair parts of itself she will conquer the West; it parts into two bunches. She borrows the outward appearance of a man, sacrifices at the Shrine of Oho-miwa until the troops assemble, puts a stone in her loins to delay her delivery, and assigns the gentle spirit to guard her life and the rough spirit to lead the van. The Wind-God and Sea-God carry her fleet to Silla; the tide follows the ships inland, and the terrified King of Silla submits with a white rope and white flag, swearing by the sun, the River Arinare and the river pebbles become stars.
summary.zh: 皇后縱髮臨海誓曰：賴天神地祇皇祖之靈西征，若濟則髮自分為兩。入海而浴，髮果自析。乃以男裝行男略，祭大神宮而兵集，納石於腰祈事畢乃產，以和魂護身、荒魂為前軍。發對馬，風伯起風，海神鼓浪，大魚蔽浮，不勞楫而達新羅，海潮隨船深入其國。新羅王自縛請降，誓以東方之日、逆流之水與升星之礫，歲時貢獻。后不殺，收其圖籍，植矛於王門，八十船寶物隨軍。高句麗、百濟亦稱西蕃，是謂三韓。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Nihongi): the legendary conquest of Korea, a sensitive episode in Japanese-Korean relations; passages are condensed paraphrases of the public-domain Aston translation, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: The Empress returned to the Bay of Kashihi, and loosing her hair, looked over the sea, saying: 'I, having received the instructions of the Gods of Heaven and Earth, and trusting in the Spirits of the Imperial ancestors, floating across the deep blue sea, intend in person to chastise the West. Therefore do I now lave my head in the water of the sea. If I am to be successful, let my hair part spontaneously into two.' Accordingly she entered the sea and bathed, and her hair parted of its own accord. The Empress bound it up parted into bunches. Then she addressed her ministers: 'To make war and move troops is a matter of the greatest concern to a country. If I entrusted to you, my ministers, the duties of the expedition we are about to undertake, the blame, in case of ill-success, would rest with you. Therefore, although I am a woman, and a feeble woman too, I will for a while borrow the outward appearance of a man, and force myself to adopt manly counsels. Above, I shall receive support from the Spirits of the Gods of Heaven and Earth, while below I shall avail myself of the assistance of you, my ministers.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book IX, secs. 7-8 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: The various provinces were ordered to collect ships and practise the use of weapons, but an army could not be assembled. The Empress said: 'This is surely the will of a God.' So she erected the Shrine of Oho-miwa and offered there a sword and a spear, and then the troops assembled freely. A fisherman of Ahe sent out into the Western Sea to spy for land saw none; then a fisherman of Shika, after several days, reported: 'To the north-west there is a mountain girt with clouds and extending crosswise. This is perhaps a country.' A lucky day was fixed by divination, and the Empress, grasping her battle-axe, commanded the three divisions of her army: 'Spare not the violent, slay not the submissive. There will surely be rewards for those who ultimately conquer in battle, and punishments for those who turn their backs and flee.' After this a God gave instructions, saying: 'A gentle spirit will attach itself to the Empress's person and keep watch over her life: a rough spirit will form the vanguard and be a guide to the squadron.' The time for the Empress's delivery having come, she took a stone which she inserted in her loins and prayed: 'Let my delivery be in this land on the day that I return after our enterprise is at an end.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book IX, secs. 8-9 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: Sail was set from the harbour of Wani in Tsushima. Then the Wind-God made a breeze to spring up, and the Sea-God uplifted the billows. The great fishes of the ocean, every one, came to the surface and encompassed the ships. A great wind blew from a favourable quarter, and following the waves, without the labour of oar or helm, they arrived at Silla. The tide-wave following the ships reached far up into the interior of the country. The King of Silla feared and trembled, and said to his people: 'Since the State of Silla was founded it has never yet been heard that the water of the sea has encroached upon the land. Is it possible that the term of existence granted to it by Heaven has expired, and that our country is to become a part of the ocean?' Scarce had he spoken when a warlike fleet overspread the sea, their banners resplendent in the sunlight.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book IX, secs. 10-11 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: The King of Silla said: 'I have heard that in the East there is a divine country named Nippon, and also that there is there a wise sovereign called the Tenno. This divine force must belong to that country. How could we resist them by force of arms?' So he took a white flag, and of his own accord rendered submission, tying his hands behind his back with a white rope. He sealed up the maps and registers, and going down before the Royal vessel bowed his head to the ground: 'Henceforward, as long as Heaven and Earth endure, we will obediently act as thy forage-providers. Not allowing the helms of our ships to become dry, every spring and every autumn we will send tribute of horse-combs and whips; and, without thinking the sea-distance a trouble, we will pay annual dues of male and female slaves.' He confirmed this by repeated oaths: 'When the sun no longer rises in the East but comes forth in the West; when the River Arinare turns its course backward, and when the river pebbles ascend and become stars - if before this we fail to pay homage every spring and every autumn, may the Gods of Heaven and Earth both together punish us.' Someone said: 'Let us put to death the King of Silla.' The Empress answered that having received the divine promise of the Land of Gold and Silver, and given orders to slay not the submissive, it would be unlucky to kill them: she loosed his cords and made him her forage-provider. She placed seals on the magazines of precious treasure, took possession of the books of maps and registers, and the spear on which she leant was planted at the gate of the King of Silla as a memorial to after ages. Phasa Mikeun, King of Silla, gave a hostage and loaded eighty vessels with gold, silver, bright colours, figured gauzes and silks; and the kings of Koryo and Pekche, finding the warlike power of the Empress invincible, declared themselves her western frontier provinces - what is termed the three Han.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book IX, secs. 11-12 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

title.en: The Birth of Homuda in the Land He Was Promised
title.zh: 譽田別天皇誕於所諾之地

region.en: Umi in Tsukushi, on the return from Silla

source.work: Nihongi (Chronicles of Japan), Vol. I, trans. W. G. Aston (1896)

summary.en: Fulfilling the oracle that the child in the Empress's womb should possess the Land of Treasure, Jingu gives birth to the future Emperor Homuda (Ojin) in Tsukushi on the return from Silla; the place is called Umi, Birth. A variant version gives the whole arc in Chuai's lifetime: gods speaking through mediums and the Empress's lute-playing, the offer of the dazzling land, the Emperor's disbelief and death the same night, and the sea-wave that followed the ships into Silla.
summary.zh: 神功皇后自新羅還，十二月十四日於筑紫生譽田別天皇，故名其地曰宇美。天皇生而臂上有肉，形如韛肘，后以為男之韛肘，因號譽田別。在胎之時天神地祇已以三韓屬之。一說仲哀之世神憑皇后彈琴而誨帝，帝不信，其夜而崩，神乃許以腹中之子得寶國。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Nihongi); passages are condensed paraphrases of the public-domain Aston translation, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: The Empress returned from Silla. In the twelfth month, fourteenth day, she gave birth to the Emperor Homuda in Tsukushi. Therefore the men of that time called the place where he was born Umi, Birth. The Emperor Homuda was the fourth child of the Emperor Tarashi Nakatsu-hiko; his mother's name was Okinaga Tarashi-hime no Mikoto. When he was born there was flesh growing on his arm in shape like an elbow-pad, and as to this resemblance the Empress judged that it was the elbow-pad worn as a manly accoutrement: therefore he was styled by this name and called the Emperor Homuda. Before this time, when the Emperor was in the womb, the Gods of Heaven and Earth had granted to him the three Han.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Books IX-X (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: One version says: 'When the Emperor Tarashi-nakatsu-hiko dwelt in the palace of Kashihi in Tsukushi, there were Deities who spoke by the mouth of Uchi-saru-taka, Kuni-saru-taka and Matsu-ya-tane, ancestors of the Agata-nushi of Saha, and admonished the Emperor: If the august descendant wishes to gain the Land of Treasure, we will presently bestow it on him. So on a later day a lute was brought and given to the Empress, and she played upon it in accordance with the word of the Gods. Hereupon the Gods spoke by the mouth of the Empress and admonished the Emperor, saying: The land which the august descendant wishes for is, as it were, a stag's horn and not a real country. But if the august descendant now makes due offering to us of the ship in which he sails, and of the water-field called Ohota given him as tribute by Homutate, the Atahe of Anato, we will bestow on him a dazzling land, a land of plenteous treasures, fair to look upon as a beautiful woman.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book IX, sec. 13 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Emperor answered the Gods: Gods though ye may be, why these deceiving words? Where is there any country? Nor do I know what Gods ye are: I pray you, let me know your names. Then the Gods gave their names, Uha-tsutsu no wo, Naka-tsutsu no wo, Soko-tsutsu no wo, and again one said: I am Mukahitsu no wo, Kiki-so-ofu-itsu-no mitama, Hayasa-nobori no Mikoto. The Emperor spoke to the Empress: What ill-sounding things they say! Is it a woman? What is meant by Hayasa-nobori? Then the Gods addressed the Emperor: O King, since thou art thus unbelieving, thou shalt not possess that country. But the child which is now in the Empress's womb, he will doubtless take possession of it. On that night the Emperor took suddenly ill and died. Afterwards the Empress performed worship in accordance with the directions of the Gods, then clad in male attire went on the expedition against Silla, and the Gods guided her: the wave which followed the ship reached far into the interior of the Land of Silla.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book IX, sec. 13 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

title.en: The Revolt of Prince Oshikuma and the Cut Bow-Strings
title.zh: 忍熊王之叛與斷弦之計

region.en: Uji river and the Seta crossing, Afumi (Lake Biwa)

source.work: Nihongi (Chronicles of Japan), Vol. I, trans. W. G. Aston (1896)

summary.en: Princes Kakosaka and Oshikuma, Chuai's elder sons, plot against the newborn heir while Jingu is in Korea: they raise a misasagi at Akashi with stones rafted from Awaji. At a hunt-prayer a wild boar leaps on Kakosaka and kills him. Oshikuma waits at Sumiyoshi; Takechi no Sukune deceives him into cutting every bow-string and flinging every sword into the river, then reveals spare strings hidden in the top-knots and real swords, routs him at Afusaka, and pursues him to the Seta crossing, where the Prince and Isachi no Sukune drown together like grebes.
summary.zh: 香坂王與忍熊王聞帝崩、后西征又生皇子，謀叛。借營山陵之名至播磨作明石陵，連舟運淡路之石，執兵以待后。獵祈於兔寸野，忽有赤豕突起噬香坂王而卒。忍熊王退屯住吉。后遣武內宿禰等率數萬擊之。宿禰密令全軍藏副弦於髻，佩木劍，詐謂各斷弦棄兵以示和，王信而全軍斷弦投河。宿禰軍復弦佩真劍渡河擊之，破於逢坂，追至栗隅柴，血流入栗隅村，故至今栗隅之果不薦於御膳。王與狹穗彥弟彥宿禰同沉瀨田渡而死。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Nihongi); passages are condensed paraphrases of the public-domain Aston translation, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Now Prince Kakosaka and Prince Oshikuma, hearing of the Emperor's decease, as well as of the Empress's expedition to the West, and of the recent birth of an Imperial Prince, plotted secretly, saying: 'The Empress has now a child, and all the ministers obey her. They will certainly consult together and establish an infant sovereign. But shall we, the elders, obey our younger brother?' So, pretending that it was in order to build a misasagi for the Emperor, they went to Harima and raised a misasagi at Akashi, joining boats together in a string across to the island of Ahaji and transporting the stones of that island to build it. Now they made every man take a weapon, and so awaited the Empress. Hereupon Kurami-wake, ancestor of the Kimi of Inugami, and Isachi no Sukune, ancestor of the Kishi, joined themselves unto Prince Kakosaka, who made them his generals.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book IX, sec. 18 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: The two Princes went forth together to the moor of Toga and made a hunt-prayer, saying: 'If our project is to be successful, then surely let us take some good game.' The two Princes sat each in his shelter, when a wild-boar sprang out suddenly, and climbing on to the shelter, bit Prince Kakosaka and killed him. The soldiers every one shuddered with fear. Then Prince Oshikuma addressed Kurami-wake: 'This is a very ominous thing. We ought not to await the enemy here.' So he withdrew his troops and encamped at Sumiyoshi. At this time the Empress heard that Prince Oshikuma had raised an army and was awaiting her. She commanded Takechi no Sukune to take in his bosom the Imperial Prince and go out across by way of the south-sea provinces to anchor in the harbour of Kii, while the Empress's ship made straight for Naniha. At this time the Empress's ship swerved towards the midst of the sea and was unable to proceed; she returned to the harbour of Muko and made divination, and the Gods instructed her where each should be enshrined, so that she was enabled to cross the sea in peace.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book IX, secs. 18-19 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Empress commanded Takechi no Sukune and Take-furu-kuma to lead an army of several tens of thousands of men to attack Prince Oshikuma. They went out by way of Yamashiro as far as Uji and encamped north of the river. Kuma-no-Kori, who formed the vanguard of Oshikuma's army, encouraged his men with a loud song of the pine-clad plain beyond the river. Then Takechi no Sukune made an order that every man should bind his hair mallet-wise, conceal spare bow-strings in his top-knot, and gird on wooden swords; then he deluded Prince Oshikuma, saying: 'I am not greedy to possess the Empire. Only, while cherishing the infant Prince, we will obey my Lord the Prince. I pray thee let us both cut our bow-strings, fling away our weapons, and be in harmony together.' So he openly gave orders to his army to cut their bow-strings and fling their swords into the river. Prince Oshikuma believed these deluding words and ordered all his troops to do likewise. Upon this Takechi no Sukune commanded the three divisions of his army to produce their spare bow-strings, string their bows again, and, girt with their real swords, advance across the river.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book IX, secs. 20-21 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: Prince Oshikuma, seeing that he had been deceived, said to Kurami-wake and Isachi no Sukune: 'We have been deceived, and have now no spare weapons. How shall we be able to fight?' He withdrew his forces and gradually retreated; Takechi sent forth his choice troops, came up with him at Afusaka and put him to the rout. The army took to flight and ran as far as Kurusu in Sasanami, where many were slain; the blood overflowed into Kurusu, and in horror of this, until this day, the fruit of Kurusu is not offered to the Imperial Palace. Prince Oshikuma, not knowing whither to betake himself in his flight, called to him Isachi no Sukune and made a song: 'Come, my child Isachi Sukune! Rather than receive a severe wound from the mallet of Uchi no Aso, like unto the grebe let us make a plunge!' So they sank together in the crossing-place of Seta and died. Takechi no Sukune made a song over the birds that dived at the ferry of Seta: 'Since with my eyes I cannot see them, can they be still alive?' Several days after they came out on the river-bank at Uji, and Takechi made a song: 'Passing Tanakami, have been caught at Uji.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book IX, sec. 21 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

title.en: The Eternal Night: Two Priests Buried in One Grave
title.zh: 晝如夜之咎與神靈託地

region.en: Muko harbour and Shinu palace, Kahachi

source.work: Nihongi (Chronicles of Japan), Vol. I, trans. W. G. Aston (1896)

summary.en: Sailing for Naniha to meet the rebels, the Empress's ship swerves into mid-sea and will not move; divination at Muko brings instructions from four deities - Amaterasu's rough spirit, Waka-hiru-me, Koto-shiro-nushi and the three water-gods - each naming the land where he wishes to be worshipped, and only then can she cross in peace. Later, at the palace of Shinu, the day is dark as night for many days; an old man explains it is the calamity of the two priests of Shinu and Amano, friends buried in one grave; the tombs are opened and re-interred separately, and daylight returns.
summary.zh: 后舟向浪速而漂於海心不得進，還武庫而卜。天照大神荒魂、稚日霙姬、事代主神與水底三神各託辭求祀地，后依而祀之乃得安渡。至忍宮，晝如夜者多日。野老曰此乃忍神與天神二神主同穴而葬之咎。發墓視之果然，乃改葬各異其棺，日光乃出。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Nihongi); passages are condensed paraphrases of the public-domain Aston translation, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: At this time the Empress's ship swerved towards the midst of the sea, and was unable to proceed. She returned again to the harbour of Muko, where she made divination as to this. Hereupon Ama-terasu no Oho-kami admonished her, saying: 'My rough spirit may not approach the Imperial residence. Let him dwell in the land of Hirota in Mikokoro.' So Hayama-hime, daughter of Yamashiro-neko, was appointed to worship him. Moreover, Waka-hiru-me no Mikoto admonished the Empress, saying: 'I wish to dwell in the land of Nagawo in Ikuta.' So Una-gami no Isachi was appointed to worship her. Again, Koto-shiro-nushi no Mikoto admonished her, saying: 'Worship me in the land of Nakata in Mikokoro.' So Naga-hime, younger sister of Hayama-hime, was appointed to worship him. Again the three Gods, Uha-tsutsu no wo, Naka-tsutsu no wo, and Soko-tsutsu no wo, admonished her, saying: 'Let our gentle spirits dwell at Nagawo in Nunakura in Ohotsu, so that they may look upon the ships passing back and forward.' Hereupon these Gods were enshrined in accordance with their instructions, and the Empress was enabled to cross the sea in peace.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book IX, sec. 19 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Empress proceeded southwards to the land of Kii, and met the Prince Imperial at Hitaka. She removed to the Palace of Shinu. It so happened that at this time the day was dark like night. Many days passed in this manner, and the men of that time said: 'This is the Eternal Night.' The Empress inquired of Toyomimi, the ancestor of the Atahe of Ki, saying: 'Wherefore is this omen?' Then there was an old man who said: 'I have heard by tradition that this kind of omen is called Atsunahi no tsumi.' She inquired what it meant. He answered: 'The priests of the two shrines have been buried together.' Therefore she made strict investigation in the village.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book IX, secs. 19-20 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: There was a man who said: 'The priest of Shinu and the priest of Amano were good friends. The priest of Shinu fell ill and died. The priest of Amano wept and wailed, saying: We have been friends together since our birth. Why in our death should there not be the same grave for both? So he lay down beside the corpse and died of himself, so that they were buried together. This is perhaps the reason.' So they opened the tomb, and on examination found that it was true. Therefore they again changed their coffins and interred them separately, upon which the sunlight shone forth, and there was a difference between day and night.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book IX, secs. 19-20 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

title.en: A-chik-ki and Wang-in: The Coming of Chinese Learning
title.zh: 阿直岐與王仁：漢學東漸

region.en: Court at Naniha and Karu, Yamato

source.work: Nihongi (Chronicles of Japan), Vol. I, trans. W. G. Aston (1896)

summary.en: The King of Pekche sends A-chik-ki with two quiet horses as tribute; they are stabled at the acclivity of Karu, named Mumaya-saka, Stable-hill. A-chik-ki is able to read the classics and becomes teacher to the Heir Apparent. Asked whether any learned man is his superior, he names Wang-in of Pekche; envoys are sent to summon him, and Wang-in arrives to teach the prince the classical books - the beginning of Chinese learning in Japan.
summary.zh: 百濟王貢良馬二匹，牧於輕坂，因名廄坂。阿直岐能讀經典，為菟道稚郎子之師。帝問更有勝汝之博士乎，對曰有王仁。乃遣上毛野君等往百濟徵之。王仁至，皇子受諸書，無不通曉，是為漢學之始。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Nihongi); Aston dates this transmission of writing 120 years later; passages are condensed paraphrases of the public-domain Aston translation, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: The King of Pekche sent A-chik-ki with two quiet horses as tribute. So they were fed in stables on the acclivity of Karu, and A-chik-ki was appointed to have charge of their foddering. Therefore the place where the horses were kept was named Mumaya-saka, Stable-hill. Moreover, A-chik-ki was able to read the classics, and so the Heir Apparent made him his teacher. Hereupon the Emperor inquired of A-chik-ki, saying: 'Are there other learned men superior to thee?' He answered and said: 'There is Wang-in, who is superior.' Then Areda wake, ancestor of the Kimi of Kodzuke, and Kamu-nagi wake were sent to Pekche to summon Wang-in.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book X, sec. 15 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: Wang-in arrived, and straightway the Heir Apparent took him as teacher and learnt various books from him. There was none which he did not thoroughly understand. Therefore the man called Wang-in was the first ancestor of the Fumi no Obito, the chiefs of writing. In the same year King Ahwa of Pekche died, and the Emperor sent for Prince Tyen-chi and addressed him: 'Do thou return to thy country and succeed to the royal Dignity.' Accordingly he further granted to him the territory of Eastern Han and so dismissed him. Meanwhile, Kidzu no Sukune of Heguri and Tada no Sukune of Ikuba had been sent to Kara with choice troops to assail Silla and open a way for Sotsuhiko, whose return had been long delayed: the King of Silla was afraid, confessed his guilt, and they brought away with them the people of Kungwol and Sotsuhiko.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book X, secs. 15-16 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the twentieth year, autumn, ninth month, Achi no Omi, ancestor of the Atahe of the Aya of Yamato, and his son Tsuga no Omi immigrated to Japan, bringing with them a company of their people of seventeen districts. Earlier, in the fourteenth year, the King of Pekche had sent as tribute a seamstress named Maketsu, first ancestress of the seamstresses of Kume; and the Lord of Yutsuki came from Pekche to offer his allegiance, saying that, coming with one hundred and twenty districts of the people of his own land, the men of Silla had prevented them and forced them to remain in the land of Kara. Katsuraki no Sotsuhiko was sent to bring the men of Yutsuki from Kara, but three years passed and he did not come.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book X, secs. 14 and 20 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.
